extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers of an early-18th-century periodical interested in manners, theatre, family life, and morals
extracted.subtask_short: spectator essays on taste and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: A series of Spectator essays (early-18th-century periodical pieces) offering prescriptive judgments and standards about family life, mourning, theatre/audience behaviour, church decorum, and the varieties of wit. The pages are essays aiming to instruct readers in good taste and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patriarchal family as a small sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: The master of a family is likened to a 'Patriarchal Sovereignty' — both king and priest — administering rewards and punishments within the household and acting as a deputy-governor over one’s parcel of subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat family government as a legitimate small-scale polity; take pleasure and responsibility in domestic administration. (Original phrasing: 'I look upon my Family as a Patriarchal Sovereignty... I am my self both King and Priest.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of having a multitude of children
rubrics_metrics.description: Having many children is presented as an accidental advantage and a great blessing — a source of pride, perpetuation, and public benefit; producing virtuous citizens and Christians is counted higher than material or artistic achievements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recounts rejoicing in 'a little Troop' and compares offspring to greater monuments; the metric of success includes producing 'reasonable Creatures, Citizens, and Christians.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Education of children: equal planting of industry and honest principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The best endowment a parent can give each child is a virtuous education: 'to implant in every one of my Children the same Seeds of Industry, and the same honest Principles.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid spoiling the eldest or pampering the youngest (per Bacon). The practical aim is to give each child a fair chance so at least one may prosper in army, navy, trade, or professions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coping with grief: patience as a necessary companion
rubrics_metrics.description: In the allegory of the Island of Grief, 'Patience' is the prudent companion who deters rash actions, accompanies sufferers, administers comfort and advice, and helps them avoid the worst dangers of the voyage through sorrow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: yielding to impatience or solitary frenzy (e.g., attempting suicide) worsens the condition. Positive practices: keep company, share stories, receive mutual pity, and accept 'Gleams of Amusement' to let reason contend with passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of indulging in the centre of grief (the Grotto)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Grotto of Grief—brooding gloom, thorns, and paralyzing melancholy—symbolizes the peril of dwelling at the deepest point of sorrow where reason is overwhelmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid penetrating into the most 'dusky silent' part of grief; follow Patience's advice to ascend out of the mournful dale, seek lighter company, and permit Comfort to restore perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good public taste: approval of sober, humane sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A people who spontaneously and universally applaud humane, sober sentiment (e.g., 'I am a Man, and cannot help feeling any Sorrow that can arrive at Man') demonstrate 'the greatest Humanity' and good understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use audience reaction to judge national disposition; preference for elevated sentimens over bawdy or mere physical amusement is a hallmark of refined taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage material should not oppose virtue or good manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage may present indifferent matters, provided they 'have nothing against the Interests of Virtue' and are not offensive to good manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible examples: well-drawn rusticities, comic portraits like Dogget's Hob. Forbidden/criticized elements: obscene sexual display that reduces audiences to chuckles, gratuitous sensationalism (entrances of ghosts, embattling of armies, noisy displays of heroes in love) when they serve only to excite coarse appetites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors must respect the author's sentiment and avoid ad-libbing
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an 'intolerable Folly' for players to put in words of their own; such confidence feeds and reinforces the audience's absurd taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Players should not improvise lines that corrupt the author's intent; excessive actor-ad-libbing is an anti-pattern that encourages low humour and disrupts proper theatrical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors should value applause of the reasonable company, not fools
rubrics_metrics.description: Players who prefer the applause of fools or coxcombs to the approval of the 'reasonable part of the Company' are blameworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek the approval of thoughtful spectators; courting the vulgar roar of the gross crowd corrupts performance and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience decorum: spectators should not behave as showy coxcombs
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Cluster of Coxcombs' who attend primarily to show themselves insult actors and other audience members; such people 'come only to shew themselves' and have no genuine regard for the performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences should refrain from interrupting, displaying lascivious voyeurism (e.g., chuckling at sex-scenes), or otherwise reducing theatre to a spectacle for vanity. Deference and restraint are marks of good attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church decorum: avoid ostentation and distraction in worship
rubrics_metrics.description: In church, ostentatious dress, affectation, and behaviour that divert the congregation (e.g., standing a whole service to show the figure, monopolizing singing, extravagant gestures) are improper and disturbing to sober devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend with sobriety; avoid coming to other parishes to exhibit oneself. The letter 'Phantom' illustrates distracting conduct (standing throughout service, dominating musical moments, theatrical gestures) as an offence to collective worship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of wit: mechanical devices (puns, crambo) are low; genuine wit requires capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Punning, cross-purposes, crambo, and mechanical verse-shapes are amusements for those with small capacities; superior wit consists in making actual verses or producing elegant, natural sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cheap wordplay as a substitute for true wit. Cultivate capacity for thoughtful expression ('those who can make Verses') and breeding that prevents indecorous double-meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-meaners and indecent allusions are breaches of breeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who supply lack of wit with a lack of breeding by indulging in immodest double-meanings offend especially women and the well-bred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from sexual innuendo and low raillery in mixed company; such behaviour gains approval only among the unbred and is socially corrosive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biting (deceitful teasing) is knavish and pernicious
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Biter' tells someone something seemingly credible, elicits a serious response, then cries 'Bite' to reveal it was a jest—this practice depends on deceit and treats the duped as a fool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biting is a form of knavery that relies on deceiving the unsuspecting; it is condemned as frivolous and pernicious. Examples given include social 'bites' at court and an anecdote of the condemned man tricking a surgeon.
